The published program finds them by walking the 24 hours and, for each, solving 5.5m = 30*(h mod 12) +- alpha for the minute offset m by cases on the hour, holding m exactly as a quotient and a remainder over 11 and discarding any m of 60 or more; a candidate is counted when its whole-minute part lies inside the window, except at the closing minute, where a nonzero remainder places the instant strictly after the window and is rejected. That endpoint rule is what makes the inclusive bounds correct, since the fractional part can only push an instant later. Each query costs O(24) time and O(1) space, trivially inside the limits for t <= 100 queries.
problems.statement_summary: Given a start time, an end time and an angle that is zero, ninety or a hundred and eighty degrees, the task is to count the instants in the closed interval at which the hour and minute hands of a continuously moving analogue clock form exactly that angle. Both times fall within one day, and up to one hundred such queries are asked.

problems.solution: For each query let L and R be the u-th and v-th smallest values of the subarray; the editorial reaches them with a wavelet tree, but a persistent segment tree over the compressed values answers the same order-statistic, rank and multiplicity queries and is what was implemented and tested. If L equals R the window is a single repeated value and the answer is immediate; otherwise every value strictly between L and R contributes its entire multiplicity, because its sorted block lies between L's block, which reaches position u, and R's block, which begins at or before v, so only L and R are clipped and their clipped counts follow from two rank queries - a step the editorial's prose leaves out, although its code performs it. What remains is, for i equal to 1, 2 and 3, the bitwise or of the values strictly between L and R occurring at least i times in the subarray, and the bits are independent: bit k is set exactly when some qualifying value carries it. Processing queries offline in decreasing left endpoint, maintain for every value the position of its i-th occurrence at or after the current left endpoint, so 'occurs at least i times in the range' becomes 'that position is at most r'; one segment tree per pair of level and bit over the compressed value axis, holding the minimum of those positions across the values carrying that bit, answers each bit with a single range-minimum over the compressed interval strictly between L and R. Advancing the left endpoint by one shifts exactly one value's three tracked positions, so maintenance is O(1) structures touched per bit per step. Total cost is O(30 (n+q) log n) time and O(30 n) space, which fits the summed limits of two hundred thousand on n and on q.
problems.statement_summary: An array of up to two hundred thousand integers is given together with as many queries. Each query names a contiguous range and a window of positions within that range once the range has been sorted, and asks for the sum of three bitwise ors: over the values occurring at least once, at least twice, and at least three times inside that sorted window. The array is never modified.

problems.solution: Sort the edges by weight and run Kruskal one whole weight class at a time, keeping a DSU that has absorbed everything strictly lighter. An edge of the class whose endpoints are already in the same component lies in no minimum spanning tree and can never create an alternative one, so it is kept for free; the rest join distinct components, and since they all share a weight the MST is unique only if they form a forest, so exactly the ones that close a cycle among themselves are deleted. That set is optimal: in any surviving graph with a unique MST, every non-tree edge must be strictly heavier than its whole tree path (otherwise swapping gives a second MST), so its endpoints are already joined by lighter edges and it is one of the free edges, bounding the survivors by (n-1) plus the number of free edges; the construction reaches that bound, and because only cycle-closing edges are dropped the graph stays connected and every weight prefix keeps exactly the components it had, so the classes really are independent. A disconnected input is detected by a preliminary union of all edges and answered with -1. Sorting dominates, giving O(m log m) time and O(n+m) space for m up to 3*10^5 summed over test cases.
problems.statement_summary: A student has drawn an undirected weighted graph that may admit several minimum spanning trees. He wants to delete as few edges as possible so that exactly one minimum spanning tree remains; the weight deleted is irrelevant. The task is to report that minimum count and one such set of edges, or to report that the graph is disconnected. Graphs carry up to three hundred thousand edges.

problems.solution: Increments only raise a number and a rearrangement cannot change how many digits it has, so the cheapest route to a c-digit target first climbs to the smallest c-digit number, 10^(c-1), at a fixed toll of 5(c-1)^2+4(c-1) instructions, and then assembles the target's digit multiset one digit at a time: increment the units digit from zero up to the wanted value, then spend one rearrangement to shove it aside. The published code collapses that into a closed form: the base toll, plus for each digit its value plus one, with three rebates - the leading 1 of 10^(c-1) already supplies one digit '1' free, the last digit placed needs no closing rearrangement, and when the target contains no digit 1 at all the spare 1 is grown into the leading digit instead. Targets shaped as a digit d followed by zeros are the exception for d of at least 2, since the only way in is an increment from (d-1) followed by nines, so they cost the base toll plus d-1 plus 10(c-1), one less when d is 2; the case d equal to 1 is not an exception at all, because 10^(c-1) is where the climb already ends and so costs exactly the base toll. Single-digit targets cost x-1. Each of the up to 1000 queries is therefore answered in O(number of digits) = O(1) time and O(1) space. A 0-1 BFS over the true state graph (v -> v+1 at cost 1, v -> its digit-multiset class at cost 1, class -> every member at cost 0, restricted to numbers with at most c digits, which is safe because digit count never decreases) reproduces the formula exactly for every x of at most seven digits, all 9,999,999 of them, with zero mismatches. Inputs of eight to ten digits are not checked against the search, which would not fit in memory; they rest on the toll being linear in the digit count, which the seven checked decades establish but do not prove.
problems.statement_summary: Starting from the number one, a machine may either add one to its current value or rearrange that value's decimal digits into any order that does not begin with a zero. For up to a thousand targets, each as large as one billion, the task is to report the fewest such instructions needed to turn one into the given target.

problems.solution: The board is at most six by six, so the solutions can simply be enumerated. The published program lays the rows down one at a time: within a row it places the clue's blocks left to right in every position that keeps them in order with at least one white cell between consecutive blocks, recursing on the triple (row, next free column, index of the next block), and an empty clue leaves the row white. Every row it completes therefore satisfies its own clue by construction, so when all rows are down it only has to read the run lengths off each of the c columns and compare them with the column clues, incrementing the counter on a full match. The enumeration is exhaustive because the correspondence between a line matching a clue and an ordered choice of block start positions is a bijection. The widest row has only ten placements (a clue of two singletons in six columns is the maximum), bounding the search by ten to the sixth leaves and O(r*c) work per leaf, roughly three times ten to the seventh operations worst case; that adversarial input measured 0.08 s, and space is O(r*c).
problems.statement_summary: A nonogram board with at most six rows and six columns comes with a clue for every row and every column: the lengths, in order, of the maximal blocks of black cells in that line, with at least one white cell separating consecutive blocks. The task is to count the black-and-white colourings of the board that satisfy every row clue and every column clue simultaneously.

problems.solution: A query returns the image of the queried switch set under the hidden permutation, so a fixed family of sets that separates every switch index is enough to identify each source's switch. The published solution runs the segment-tree recursion over the switch range and asks, once per depth, a single query holding the union of all left-child intervals at that depth; because those are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from every right-child interval at the same depth, the depth-(d+1) reply cleanly splits the set of sources already attributed to a node into the part driven by its left half (present in that reply) and the part driven by its right half (absent), and recursing to the leaves names the switch of every source. That is one query per level, ceiling(log2 n)+1, which is at most 11 for n up to 1000 and well inside the budget of 32; the queries are non-adaptive and carry exactly the same information as asking, for each bit position, the set of switches whose index has that bit set. Correctness needs no assumption about lamp state because the reply reports which sources were toggled, not whether they are lit. Work is O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space for the per-depth query sets. A transcription driven against a simulated interactor recovers the permutation for every permutation with n at most 6 and for 400 random sizes up to 1000, never exceeding 11 queries, and always agrees with the bitwise solution.
problems.statement_summary: A butler faces switches, each controlling exactly one of an equal number of light sources, but the pairing is unknown. In one round he may flip any non-empty set of switches and is then told, in arbitrary order, which sources changed state. With up to a thousand switches and at most thirty-two rounds allowed, he must report which switch drives each source.

problems.solution: Run Dijkstra four times, from each house and each school, and then classify every vertex and every edge once. A walker occupies a point p only at time dist(house, p), and only when dist(house, p) + dist(p, school) equals the shortest distance; the school vertex is additionally occupied at every later time because they wait there forever. So a vertex counts when it lies on shortest paths of both and the two arrival times are equal, or when it is one walker's school, lies on the other's shortest paths, and the other passes it no earlier than its owner arrives. Since every weight is positive, an edge can lie on a given walker's shortest paths in at most one direction, so the only interior meetings are head-on: if one enters at time a and the other enters from the far end at time c on an edge of length w, they cross at the single point reached at time (a+c+w)/2, which is strictly inside the edge exactly when the absolute difference of a and c is below w, the boundary case being a vertex meeting already counted. Infinitely many meeting points can only come from traversing a whole edge together, which requires a vertex with equal arrival times having an incident edge on both walkers' shortest paths in the same direction; any finite answer is at most n+m, far under the stated billion threshold, so that test is exactly when to print -1. Four Dijkstras dominate: O((n+m) log n) time and O(n+m) space for n, m up to 5*10^5.
problems.statement_summary: Two students leave home at the same moment and walk to their schools across a weighted undirected graph, each taking some shortest route at the same speed and staying at school after arriving. The task is to count the distinct locations, on edges as well as at vertices, where the two could be present simultaneously, or report that the count would exceed a billion.

problems.solution: The recurrence is self-similar: the term equals its own index exactly at the indices b = (3^k+1)/2, that is 1, 2, 5, 14, 41, and so on, and the block of indices from b to 3b-2 interleaves a descending run b, b-1, down to 1 with an ascending run 2b, 2b+1, up to 3b-2, after which index 3b-1 holds the value 3b-1 and starts the next block. The first n terms are therefore a multiset built from O(log n) explicit integer intervals, two per complete block plus a truncated pair for the final partial block, so the number of terms not exceeding x is a short sum of interval intersections and the m-th smallest is the least x whose count reaches m, located by binary search over the value range up to 3n. Correctness rests entirely on the block identity, which follows by induction from the two-case rule, and the partial block needs no special casing at its right end because the value that continues the ascending run past 3b-2 is exactly the next block's opening value. Each query costs O(log^2 n) time and O(log n) space, so all 10^4 queries at n = 10^18 finish in a fraction of a second, and the largest reachable answer is about 1.5n, still inside signed 64-bit.
problems.statement_summary: A sequence begins at one, and each later term is formed from the previous one by adding the index when the term does not exceed it and subtracting the index otherwise. Given a length and a rank, each up to a quintillion, the task is to report which value occupies that rank once the first terms are sorted in non-decreasing order, for up to ten thousand queries.

problems.solution: The maximum-area triangle over a point set always has all three vertices on the convex hull, so the first step is a monotone-chain hull that drops duplicates and collinear points, leaving h <= N strictly convex vertices (if fewer than three survive the answer is 0). For each hull vertex a taken as the root, the largest triangle rooted at a is found by a rotating-calipers-style sweep: as the second vertex b walks forward around the hull, the best apex c is non-decreasing, because for a fixed base a-b the distance from c to that line is unimodal around a convex polygon, so one monotone pointer that advances c while the area does not decrease finds the optimum in amortised O(h) per root. Running that for every root gives O(N log N) for the sort and hull plus O(h^2) <= 25 million cross products at N = 5000, in O(N) memory. Areas are carried as twice-the-area integer cross products, which reach about 3.2*10^15 for coordinates bounded by 4*10^7, so 64-bit arithmetic is required and the halving is done only when printing. The tempting single-pass O(h) calipers variant that advances a, b and c together is unsound (Keikha et al. 2017, cited by the judges on slide 49), which is why the per-root loop is not collapsed.
problems.statement_summary: Given up to five thousand points with non-negative integer coordinates bounded by forty million, the task is to report the area of the largest triangle whose three corners are chosen among those points, or zero when no non-degenerate triangle exists. The points need not be distinct, arrive in no particular order and may include long collinear runs, and the reported area is accepted within a small absolute error.

problems.solution: Every pre-filled value is guaranteed to occupy exactly one cell in each row and each column, so the k written values together leave exactly n-k empty cells in every row and every column: the empty cells form an (n-k)-regular bipartite graph between rows and columns. A regular bipartite graph satisfies Hall's condition and therefore has a perfect matching, and deleting a perfect matching leaves a graph that is still regular, so the missing values can be placed one at a time without ever backtracking - for each unused value, build the graph of currently empty cells, run Kuhn's augmenting-path matching, and write the value into the matched cells. That argument also shows the answer is never NO, which is why the published code always prints YES and has its NO branch commented out. At most n values each cost one maximum matching over at most n squared edges, an O(n^4) worst-case bound, though the regularity keeps it near 2.6 n^3 edge visits on the densest input (n=100, k=0); space is O(n^2).
problems.statement_summary: A square grid of side at most one hundred is partly filled: some values have already been written, each exactly as many times as the grid has rows and never twice in a row or column. The task is to fill the remaining empty cells so every value appears exactly once in each row and column, or to report that no completion exists.

problems.solution: A converted character is absorbed into its asterisk immediately and asterisks never merge with anything, so every operation collapses an interval of the ORIGINAL string and the collapsed intervals are pairwise disjoint; an interval is collapsible exactly when its length is 3 to 5 and exactly one of its positions differs from the common letter of the others, the longer shapes being limited to x-z-x-x, x-x-z-x and x-x-z-x-x because the input already has no run of three. Maximality of the run that collapses adds an ordering constraint rather than a shape constraint: if the character immediately outside an end of the interval equals its common letter, that position must already be an asterisk, so the chosen interval touching that end must be collapsed first. The answer is therefore weighted interval scheduling with a budget of K intervals and weight equal to length, restricted to selections that admit a valid order, which holds exactly when every blocked end has the adjacent interval chosen and no adjacent pair blocks each other -- a mutual block is a 2-cycle and is the only possible cycle, since dependencies only ever run between neighbouring intervals along the line. A left-to-right DP over (next free position, operations used, and a flag saying whether an interval ends at the previous position and whether it still needs its right neighbour) enforces all of that, and because each interval eats at least three characters only min(K, n/3) operations matter, giving O(n*min(K,n/3)) time and memory, about 10^6 states for n = K = 1000 and trivially inside the limits for 50 test cases. Greedy and any incremental-in-K argument both fail here, which the judges' own example shows.
problems.statement_summary: A string of lowercase letters contains no run of three or more equal characters. An operation rewrites one character so that a run of at least three equal characters appears; that maximal run collapses into an asterisk, which is inert and never rewritten or absorbed. Using at most a thousand operations on a string of at most a thousand characters, the task is to maximise how many characters are absorbed.

problems.solution: Mark the cups 1, k+1, 2k+1, ... up to index n; there are m = ceil(n/k) of them and, because they are spaced exactly k apart, every window of k consecutive cups contains exactly one marked cup, so pouring only into marked cups turns the problem into the abstract game: distribute at most x litres among m slots, then the opponent zeroes one slot of its choice. That abstraction is also an upper bound on any strategy, because the opponent can restrict itself to the m windows covering the disjoint blocks of k cups (clipping the last window to end at cup n, which only destroys more), and then the maximum inside a block behaves exactly like a single slot. In the m-slot game the optimum is x times one plus the harmonic number of m-1: if u slots are still alive at a common level v, pouring x/u into each and losing one keeps the quantity v plus x times the harmonic number of u invariant, and the last surviving slot is topped up by the final free pour. The published solution realises exactly that: about 1900 rounds level all m marked cups towards x (refilling whichever was just drained and splitting the remaining x equally makes the common level approach x geometrically at rate 1-1/m), then at most 99 rounds pour x/u into the u slots the opponent has not yet drained, shrinking u to one, and the final pour adds x. It sends at most 1999 POUR lines, exactly x litres per round, and runs in O(rounds * m) time and O(m) space. One caveat about the published code specifically: it fixes its round budget at 1900 levelling rounds and 99 knock-out rounds, which reaches the optimum against any minimising opponent but falls to about 0.73 of it against an opponent that merely wastes turns, at k equal to 1 and n at least 47. A wasted opponent round only raises the survivors' level, so a split that reserves a few hundred knock-out rounds instead meets the bound against every opponent and is the version worth learning from.
problems.statement_summary: In an interactive, adaptive game with at most fifty cups, one player repeatedly distributes at most a fixed number of litres of milk tea among cups, after which opponents empty a window of consecutive cups of a fixed length, at most ten. He may instead end with a last distribution nobody drinks, and within two thousand rounds must guarantee some cup holds essentially the largest amount any strategy can force.

problems.solution: If i = p1^q1 * ... * pm^qm then i has exactly (q1+1)...(qm+1) divisors of which exactly m are prime, so NPF(i) = d(i) - omega(i), where d counts divisors and omega counts distinct prime divisors; that identity reproduces all four samples (100 -> 9-2 = 7, 13 -> 2-1 = 1, 12 -> 6-2 = 4, 2018 -> 4-2 = 2). Both tables are precomputed once for every value up to 2*10^6 by sieving rather than per query: the harmonic loop 'for each d, bump a counter at every multiple of d' gives d(i) in O(M log M), and the same loop restricted to primes gives omega(i) in O(M log log M) -- equivalently, skipping the primes in the first loop accumulates NPF directly. Each query is then a single array lookup, so the whole program is O(M log M + Q) time and O(M) memory; NPF never exceeds 283 on this range, so a 16-bit table of 2*10^6 entries (4 MB) is enough. The deciding constraint is the query count: with Q up to 3*10^6 and i up to 2*10^6, per-query trial division costs about 240 divisions on average and up to 1400 for a prime, so roughly 5*10^8 divisions in total even when memoised over the at most 2*10^6 distinct inputs, too slow for the 1 s limit, and the sheer I/O volume forces buffered or unformatted reading and writing.
problems.statement_summary: For each of up to three million queries the task is to report how many divisors of a given integer are not themselves prime, where that integer is at least two and at most two million. Because the queries greatly outnumber the distinct possible inputs and the input and output volume is very large, an answer must be produced in effectively constant time per query.

problems.solution: f is an iterated morphism (a D0L system): every letter c is rewritten as the fixed word T_c, and since every |T_c| >= 2 the expansion of a single letter after k rounds has length at least 2^k. Because every queried position is at most 10^15 < 2^50, at any level deeper than 50 the position is forced to lie inside the expansion of the FIRST character, so the top K-50 steps of the descent are the deterministic map g(c) = first letter of T_c, a functional graph on 26 nodes; folding it by rho/cycle detection (tail plus cycle is at most 26) yields g^(K-50)(S[0]) in O(26) time, which replaces S by that one letter and K by 50. With K' = min(K,50) the lengths L[k][c] = |f^k(c)| are then built bottom-up with saturating addition capped just above 10^15 (so the true value is recovered exactly whenever it is below the cap, which is all the descent ever compares against), one prefix pass over S decides which letter of S owns each query, and each query walks down at most 50 levels, scanning the at most 50 children per level to find the one containing the remaining offset. The whole answer for a query is thus read off without ever materialising the string, and the per-query work is bounded because the fold above level 50 is forced rather than chosen. Time is O(|S| + 26*K'*maxT + M*K'*maxT), about 3 million operations at |S| = 10^6, K = 10^15, M = 1000, and space is O(|S| + 26*K') for the prefix sums and the small length table.
problems.statement_summary: A password starts as a lowercase string of up to a million letters and is grown by simultaneously replacing every letter with a fixed word assigned to that letter, each word at least two letters long, repeating that substitution as many as a quadrillion times. For up to a thousand forgotten positions, none beyond a quadrillion, the task is to report which letter stands at each of those positions.

problems.solution: Root the target tree at the pre-placed block. Every legal history keeps the placed set connected and containing the root, because each new block must touch an existing one, so the placed set is always a root-closed subtree; hence the neighbour a new block bumps into can never be one of its children (a child's own path to the root would run through the still-absent block), and must be its parent. That pins each block's move exactly: it enters from the edge opposite its parent, travelling along its own row when the parent is horizontally adjacent and its own column otherwise, and it imposes two ordering constraints - the parent goes first, and the block itself goes before every target block on the ray from it to its entry edge. Those constraints are both necessary (just shown) and sufficient (following any order that respects them, each block finds its parent present and its ray clear, so it stops exactly where it must), so the answer is any topological order of the constraint digraph and impossibility is precisely a cycle, detected by Kahn's algorithm. Writing the ray constraints out is quadratic in the number of blocks, so every row and column gets prefix and suffix chains of auxiliary nodes and a block points at one chain node standing for its whole ray, keeping the graph at O(B) nodes and edges. Sorting blocks along rows and columns dominates, giving O(B log B) time and O(B) space, and the board is never materialised, which matters because N and M reach 4*10^5 while only B cells are occupied.
problems.statement_summary: A board starts with one block, and a move injects a new block from one of the four edges along a chosen row or column; it slides until it bumps into an existing block, and a move adding nothing is illegal. Given a target arrangement of up to four hundred thousand blocks whose cells form a tree under adjacency, the task is to decide reachability and list the moves.

problems.solution: Only extremal occurrences matter: if indices c<d<e<f witness A,B,A,B, then replacing c by the last occurrence of A before d and e by that occurrence's immediate successor, and f by the last occurrence of B anywhere, still leaves a witness, so the ordered pair (A,B) is achievable exactly when some index u lies strictly between two CONSECUTIVE occurrences p<q of A and the last occurrence of the value at u is beyond q. That turns the whole search into one range-maximum query per occurrence-gap over the array IM[i] = last occurrence of S[i], and the gaps number N-1 in total across all values, so a sparse table (or the debrief's event-sorted segment tree over the same reduction) answers each in O(1) after an O(N log N) build. The smallest achievable A is then the smallest value owning a gap whose IM-maximum exceeds that gap's right end, and for that single A one linear scan of the span from its first to its last occurrence, carrying the next occurrence of A, yields the smallest qualifying B - which is the part the debrief never addresses, since it argues existence only and the problem actually demands the lexicographically smallest pair. Correctness of the reduction is the two-line exchange argument above in both directions; a witness quadruple maps to such a (p,u,q) triple, and any such triple is itself a witness. Cost is O(N log N) time and O(N log N) space for the sparse table, or O(N) space if a segment tree is used instead, which clears N = 400000 comfortably (0.5 s in plain Python on the worst shapes tried). Verified on all three samples, against exhaustive O(N^4) quadruple search on 40000 random sequences with small alphabets, and against an independent cubic reference on 400 longer ones plus adversarial single-value-spanning shapes.
problems.statement_summary: A message is a sequence of up to four hundred thousand positive integers, none larger than the length of the sequence. The task is to decide whether some two distinct values appear in the repeating order A, B, A, B as a not necessarily contiguous subsequence, and if so to report the lexicographically smallest such ordered pair, otherwise to report that no such pair exists.

problems.solution: A simple path from B to G through C splits at C into two paths B->C and G->C that share no cell except C, and conversely, so the shortest such path is the minimum total length of two such vertex-disjoint paths. Split each cell into in and out nodes joined by a capacity-1 arc (capacity 2 for C), delete U, give each grid step cost 1, feed one unit into B and one into G from a super source and drain 2 units out of C. Costs are non-negative so no cycle appears in the flow and the two units decompose into the wanted paths; infeasible means NO, and the path string is read off the flow. Two Dijkstra augmentations with potentials give O(NM log(NM)) per test, fine for total NM <= 1e5.
problems.statement_summary: On a grid of at most one hundred by one hundred cells, a walker must travel from a start cell to a goal cell by unit steps, passing through a third marked cell somewhere on the way and never entering a fourth forbidden cell, and no cell may be visited twice. The task prints a shortest such route as a string of directions, or reports that none exists.

problems.solution: Brute force over every bipartite graph with parts up to 5 and 4 shows the Grundy value of the delete-a-vertex-or-an-edge game is exactly ((a+b) mod 2) + 2*(|E| mod 2). Socket, moving second, wins iff the XOR over the N games is 0, i.e. iff sum(a_i+b_i) is even and an even number of graphs carry an odd edge count. The low bit is fixed by the input, so the answer is 0 when sum(a_i+b_i) is odd; otherwise the edge parities are independent and uniform, exactly half of the 2^(a_i b_i) drawings of each graph being odd, so the count is 2^(sum a_i*b_i - 1) mod 1e9+7. O(N log) time with one modular exponentiation, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternately delete one vertex or one edge from any still non-empty graph among N drawn bipartite graphs, the i-th having parts of a_i and b_i vertices, and whoever cannot move loses. The task counts, modulo 1000000007, the ways to draw the edge sets so that the second player wins under optimal play, with N up to 100000 and part sizes up to 1000000000.

problems.solution: Day 1 occupies the N listed cells and every later day adds exactly the cells at edge-distance one from the occupied set, so a cell is taken on day 1 + d where d is its grid distance to the nearest listed cell. Push all N cells into one queue at distance 0 and run a single breadth-first search over the R x C grid; the answer is 1 plus the largest distance reached. Repeated input cells are absorbed by the visited check. O(RC + N) time, O(RC) space, trivially inside R, C <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: An army occupies N given cells of an R by C grid on the first day, and on each later day it also takes every cell that shares an edge with a cell taken earlier. The task reports how many days pass before the whole grid is occupied. The grid has at most 100 rows and 100 columns, and the listed cells need not be distinct.

problems.solution: Let f(x) count sprinkles in the half-ring starting at x. Sliding by one part swaps one sprinkle out for at most one in, so f changes by at most 1 per step, and f(x) + f(x+5e8) = N, so g = f - N/2 satisfies g(x+5e8) = -g(x). A discrete intermediate value argument therefore guarantees a zero of g, so the answer NO never happens. One query at x=0 orients an interval of length 5e8 whose endpoints have opposite signs; then binary search, but shrink using the probe value itself (a value v>0 at mid moves the left end to mid+v, v<0 moves the right end to mid+v) since g cannot cross within |v| steps. That reaches a single candidate in at most 28 further queries, so at most 30 interactions, inside the 30 + floor(log2(sqrt(N))) budget even at N=2.
problems.statement_summary: An interactive task on a ring divided into a billion numbered parts carrying N sprinkles, N even. The solver may ask how many sprinkles lie in any circular range of parts, and must name a half of the ring, five hundred million consecutive parts, holding exactly N/2 sprinkles, or report that no such half exists. At most thirty plus floor of log2 of root N interactions are permitted.

problems.solution: Every controlled area is a subtree, so the areas containing one berry are nested and its eater is the bird of its label whose area root is deepest; with at most seven birds per label that owner is found by scanning the label's bird list with an Euler-tour ancestor test. Making the tiny birds giant only enlarges areas - subtree(parent) becomes subtree(nearest big ancestor) - so every bird still contains its own berries and the only damage is that a same-label bird may now sit deeper. A berry must keep its eater, hence its label must equal that bird's, so each bird together with the berries it owns forms one block that is relabelled whole or not at all, and since all of them already carry the bird's label the cost of relabelling a block is its size. A relabelled block can always take a brand new label, which clashes with nothing, so the only constraints bind the blocks that KEEP a label L, pairwise: two kept birds of label L must not have equal new areas, and the deeper one must not contain a berry of the shallower one (a binary search over that bird's berries in Euler order). Labels are therefore independent, the 'no eight birds share a label' rule caps a class at seven birds, and the best kept set is the maximum-weight conflict-free subset over all 2^7 subsets; the answer is the total weight minus the kept weight. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
problems.statement_summary: A rooted tree's internal nodes are big or small; every leaf holds a labelled giant bird, tiny bird or berry. A tiny bird controls its parent's subtree, a giant bird its nearest big ancestor's, and the smallest controlling bird of matching label eats a berry. With every tiny bird turned giant and at most seven birds per label, the fewest labels must change so no berry changes eater.

problems.solution: Fibonacci mod m is purely periodic with period pi(m), so G(k,n) mod m_0 needs G(k-1,n) mod m_1 with m_1 = pi(m_0), and so on down a tower m_0, pi(m_0), pi(pi(m_0)), .... That tower always reaches a fixed point pi(M) = M within about twenty levels (24, 120, 600, 3000, 15000 and 375000 are the fixed points reached from p <= 1e6). If k is at most the tower depth D, reduce n modulo m_k and walk back up with fast-doubling Fibonacci. Otherwise every level below D uses the same modulus M, so the rest is the single map T(x) = F_x mod M iterated k-D times on Z_M; precompute T for each distinct M in O(M) (it is just the Fibonacci sequence mod M) and jump k-D steps through its functional graph, then walk the D levels back up. O(D log) per query after precomputation.
problems.statement_summary: Nesting the Fibonacci function k times starting from n gives a value the task must report modulo p, for up to a hundred thousand independent queries. Both n and k reach a quintillion while the modulus p stays at or below one million, so the nested value is astronomically large and only its residue can ever be formed.

problems.solution: Place vertices on a line with increasing potentials d_i and weight every edge (i,j) by d_j - d_i. Any walk then costs at least |d_end - d_start| with equality exactly for the index-increasing walks, so every increasing path is a shortest path and the count is a plain DAG count. For Bash take x_0..x_60 with d_i = i and all C(61,2) edges, giving 2^(i-1) paths to x_i, and join vertex 2 to x_(b+1) for every set bit b of A: 62 vertices and at most 1889 edges. For Chikapu take y_0..y_86 with only the edges y_(i-2)-y_i and y_(i-1)-y_i, giving Fib(i+1) paths to y_i, and join vertex 2 to the Zeckendorf terms of A: 88 vertices and 171 + at most 43 = at most 214 edges, exactly the stated cap. A = 0 is answered by the empty two-vertex graph.
problems.statement_summary: Given a value A up to a quintillion, the task builds two weighted simple undirected graphs in each of which the number of distinct shortest paths between vertex one and vertex two is exactly A. The first may use seventy-two vertices and 2525 edges, the second only eighty-eight vertices and 214 edges, and every edge weight must be a positive integer below a billion.

problems.solution: Cutting one head regrows a head, so move 1 is a no-op and the reachable moves are (H,T)->(H,T+1) for T>=1, (H,T)->(H-2,T) for H>=2 and (H,T)->(H+1,T-2) for T>=2. If a of the first, b of the second and c of the third are used then a = 2c - T and 2b = H + c, so the total 3c - T + (H+c)/2 is increasing in c and the optimum is the smallest c >= ceil(T/2) with c congruent to H mod 2. Such a plan is always orderable (all tail-growths first, then all tail-pairs, then all head-pairs), so with H, T >= 1 the answer is never -1. O(1) per test case, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: A knight fights a creature with H heads and T tails and may cut one head, one tail, two heads or two tails, but cutting a single head regrows a head, cutting a single tail regrows two tails, and cutting two tails grows a head. The creature dies only when both counts reach zero at once; the task is the fewest cuts, with H and T each at most 100.

problems.solution: Count the complement: strings of length n with no occurrence of P, then subtract from 2^n (and answer 0 when |P| > n). Track the set of pattern prefixes still alive as a bitmask A, where bit l means the last l characters match P[0..l-1]; appending '1' maps A to (A<<1)|1 and appending '0' maps A to ((A & starmask)<<1)|1, and a string is rejected as soon as bit m-1 would advance. That mask is exactly the Aho-Corasick state of the up to 2^15 concrete completions of P, so the reachable state count is bounded by the trie size, at most about 30*2^15; a dictionary-keyed DP over n <= 50 characters therefore runs in O(n * states) with states under 10^6. Measured worst case over adversarial patterns was 491520 (15 times 2^15, the adversarial worst case found by review; the rigorous bound is under 983040) states.
problems.statement_summary: A pattern of at most thirty characters, each either a one or a wildcard and at least half of them ones, marks a binary string of length n as valid when some substring of the string matches the pattern position by position, with wildcards matching either bit. The task counts how many distinct valid strings of length n exist, where n is at most fifty.

problems.solution: The happiness condition says every maximal simple path from every vertex is Hamiltonian and its far end is adjacent to the start, i.e. the graph is randomly Hamiltonian (randomly traceable). Those graphs are classified: only the cycle C_n, the complete bipartite K_{n,n} and the complete graph K_n. So for given N and M the answer is YES exactly when M = N, or N is even and M = (N/2)^2, or M = N(N-1)/2, and the corresponding graph is printed directly. Exhaustive search over all graphs on 3..6 vertices reproduces exactly this set of feasible M. O(M) per test case.
problems.statement_summary: Given a number of homes N and a required number of roads M, the task builds a simple undirected graph with exactly M edges so that from every vertex any walk that repeatedly steps to an arbitrary not yet visited neighbour, until it is stuck, has by then visited every vertex and can step straight back to its start. N is at most thirty; impossibility must be reported.

problems.solution: A point strictly inside the convex hull is strictly inside any triangle containing the hull, so every point must lie on the hull boundary; and each side line of such a triangle supports the hull, so the points it can carry are exactly one face of the hull - one vertex or one whole edge. Three faces cover at most six hull vertices, so a hull with seven or more vertices is immediately NO, every edge carrying a point in its interior must itself be a chosen face, and there are at most twelve faces, hence at most 220 triples to try. A side line may be pushed inward until it supports the hull without losing any point, so the outward normal of the side carrying a face may be any direction of that face's normal cone: one fixed direction for an edge, the closed arc between the two neighbouring edge normals for a vertex. Containment is then automatic and only boundedness is left, i.e. picking d1, d2, d3 from the three disjoint cyclically ordered arcs with all three ccw gaps strictly between 0 and pi; eliminating d2, then d3, then d1 from that system over the arcs collapses it to three independent tests - the ccw gap from the END of each arc to the START of the next must be below pi - each an integer cross-then-dot test on hull edge normals. Per test case the cost is the hull, O(n log n) time and O(n) space, plus O(n) classification and O(1) face triples.
problems.statement_summary: Given up to a hundred thousand integer lattice points, possibly repeated, the question is whether some triangle of positive area has every one of those points lying on its three sides, vertices included; the triangle's own corners need not be lattice points. Many such test cases arrive in one file, with half a million points in total, and each needs a yes or no answer.

problems.solution: For a fixed left endpoint l, a word T is a subsequence of S[l..r] exactly when r >= f(l,T), the end of the greedy leftmost match of T starting at l, so each query becomes 'k-th lexicographically smallest word with f(l,.) <= r'. Sort the words once by lexicographic rank and precompute next-occurrence tables over S. Group queries by l (only |S| <= 500 distinct values); for each l compute all f(l,.) in O(total word length) with the next tables, bucket the words by that value, sweep r upward inserting words into a Fenwick tree indexed by lexicographic rank, and answer each query by descending the Fenwick tree for the k-th set position. O(|S|*(n + sum|T|) + q log n) time, O(n + q + 26|S|) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given a string of at most 500 characters, a dictionary of up to 20000 words whose lengths total 80000, and up to 300000 queries, each query names a substring by its endpoints plus an index k and asks for the k-th lexicographically smallest dictionary word that appears as a subsequence of that substring. Long answers are truncated to ten characters, and missing ones reported.

problems.solution: With r red piles and w white piles the line alternates, so |r-w| <= 1 and there are two orders when r = w and one otherwise. Writing F(r) for the number of compositions of R into r parts of size 1..d and C(W-1,w-1) for the compositions of W, the answer is sum_r F(r) * (2C(W-1,r-1) + C(W-1,r-2) + C(W-1,r)). Substituting F(r) = [x^R] A(x)^r with A = x + ... + x^d and summing the three binomial series collapses everything to (1+A)^{W-1} * (1+A)^2, so K = [x^R] (1 + x + ... + x^d)^{W+1} = sum_j (-1)^j C(W+1,j) C(R - j(d+1) + W, W). That is O(R+W) factorials plus O(R/(d+1)) terms; the naive per-r inclusion-exclusion would be about 7*10^10 operations at d=3.
problems.statement_summary: R boxes of red wine and W boxes of white wine are split into non-empty single-colour piles arranged in a line so that neighbouring piles always differ in colour, and every red pile holds at most d boxes while white piles are unlimited. The task is to count the distinct arrangements modulo 10^9+7, with R and W each up to one million.

problems.solution: Count by inclusion-exclusion over the two allowed conditions. The number of length-N strings with equally many blue and red bars is C(N, N/2) for even N and zero for odd N; the number with no two adjacent blue bars is the Fibonacci value F(N+2); and the strings satisfying both have exactly N/2 blue bars, none adjacent, which is C(N/2+1, N/2) = N/2+1. So K = C(N,N/2) + F(N+2) - (N/2+1) for even N and F(N+2) for odd N. The real difficulty is the modulus: M is prime but may be far smaller than N (the samples use M=997 with N up to 10^6), so the central binomial coefficient needs Lucas' theorem digit by digit in base M. O(N + M) per dataset, O(M) space.
problems.statement_summary: A barcode is a row of N bars, each red or blue, and it is valid when the number of blue bars equals the number of red bars or no two blue bars are adjacent, or both. For up to twenty pairs of a length N up to one million and a prime modulus M up to ten million, the task is the number of valid barcodes modulo M.

problems.solution: Because every root-to-X path has increasing indices, the tree rooted at room 1 has parent(i) < i for every i >= 2, so room 1 has D_1 children and room i >= 2 has D_i - 1 children. Let c_1 = D_1, c_i = D_i - 1 and S_i = sum_{j<=i} c_j - (i-1), the number of still-unused child slots after rooms 1..i have been placed. The sequence is realisable exactly when sum c = N-1 (the handshake identity) and S_i >= 1 for every i < N, since room i+1 must attach to some earlier room with a free slot, and conversely any such attachment works because the parent index is automatically smaller. O(N) time and O(1) extra space.
problems.statement_summary: A network of N rooms is connected by N-1 tunnels forming a tree whose rooms are numbered so that indices strictly increase along every shortest path from room 1. Given the array of degrees, one per room, the task is to decide whether such a network can exist and print YES or NO, with N at most one thousand.

problems.solution: The ball model, pinned down by the samples: from cell (i,j) a '\\' wall rolls it down-right - it leaves by the right edge when j = N, and it is STUCK when cell (i,j+1) is '/' because the two diagonals meet in a V at their shared bottom corner; otherwise it enters (i+1,j+1) and exits the bottom at column j+1 when i = M. '/' is the mirror image. The V rule is what the last sample tests: flipping (4,4), a cell off the path, turns an exit into -1. For the queries, sqrt-decompose the ROWS. When M <= N a drop is simulated directly in O(M) = O(sqrt(MN)) steps; otherwise N < sqrt(MN) and rows are cut into blocks of B = sqrt(M/N) rows, each storing entry column -> exit column or dead, built in O(B*N). A drop walks M/B blocks and a flip rebuilds one block, both O(sqrt(M*N)). Total O(MN + Q sqrt(MN)) time, O(MN) space.
problems.statement_summary: A board of M rows and N columns holds one diagonal wall per cell, slanting either way. A ball dropped at the top of a column slides along the walls and either leaves sideways, jams between two walls, or reaches the bottom. Queries flip one wall or drop a ball, reporting its bottom exit column or minus one. Cell count and query count are each at most 100000.

problems.solution: Unlisted customer-gift pairs are worth zero, so this is the assignment problem: a maximum-weight (not necessarily perfect) matching in a bipartite graph with n customers on one side and m gifts on the other, both at most 1000. Pad the satisfaction matrix with zeros to a square, negate it and run the Jonker-Volgenant form of the Hungarian algorithm, which is O(min(n,m) * max(n,m)^2) on a dense 1000x1000 matrix and yields both the optimum and the assignment; dropping the zero-weight pairs from the printed answer is safe because weights are positive, so a zero pair never helps. Min-cost max-flow with Johnson potentials, one Dijkstra augmentation per matched pair, is the equivalent alternative. O(n*m) space.
problems.statement_summary: A company has m gifts and n loyal customers, and k survey cards each state how satisfied a given customer would be with a given gift; unlisted pairs are worth nothing. Every customer takes at most one gift and every gift goes to at most one customer. The task is to maximise the total satisfaction and print one optimal allocation, with m and n up to one thousand.

problems.solution: Let cost(i,j) = min over integer v of sum_{s=i..j} |a_s - v|^k; for k=1 that is the sum of absolute deviations from the median and for k=2 the sum of squares around round(mean), both O(1) from prefix sums of a and a^2 (for k=2 test both floor and ceil of the mean). Minimising over partitions into G consecutive segments is the layered DP dp[g][j] = min_i dp[g-1][i] + cost(i+1,j). The cost obeys the quadrangle inequality, so each layer is computed by divide-and-conquer optimisation (or Knuth's monotone-opt) instead of a full scan, giving O(G*N log N) time with N=2000 and O(N) space per layer; the plain O(G*N^2) would be 8*10^9.
problems.statement_summary: A non-decreasing sequence of N heights must be cut into G blocks of consecutive positions. A block costs the minimum over all integers v of the sum of |height - v| raised to the power k, where k is one or two. The task is to report the least achievable total cost over all such partitions, with N up to two thousand and G up to N.

problems.solution: Only residues mod k matter. Let c_r be the count of residue r, base0 = sum_r floor(c_r/2)*r mod k (one element out of each equal pair), z the number of residues with odd count, and S = 2*base0 + sum of the odd residues. Mirroring is optimal for both sides: the second player can answer every pick with the partner in a fixed perfect matching, which pins the final score to base0 plus one element of each mixed pair, and the first player can take one element and then mirror. That yields an O(k) rule: z = 0 gives DRAW (the score is forced to base0 and so is the opponent's); z = 1 with odd residue r forces the first player's score to base0 + r, and the outcome is read off directly; z = 2 with residues r1, r2 is FIRST when S is nonzero and base0 + r1 or base0 + r2 vanishes, else DRAW, and SECOND is impossible for even n; z >= 3 is always a DRAW. O(n + k) per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternately remove one number from a list of up to 1024 integers until it is empty, the first player starting, and each scores the sum of what he took. A player wins only if his own score is divisible by k while his opponent's is not; otherwise the game is drawn. Across datasets with k at most 32, report the result under optimal play.

problems.solution: Two cells in the same row or column must get the same real level when their virtual heights are equal and a strictly larger one when the virtual height is larger. Union-find the equal pairs (sort each row and each column and merge neighbouring equal entries), then add, between consecutive distinct values of each sorted row and column, one edge from the smaller component to the larger one; transitivity covers the rest, so the edge count stays O(mn). The minimum number of levels is the length of the longest chain, i.e. the longest path in that DAG, obtained by a topological-order DP that sets level(v) = 1 + max level over predecessors; the answer is the maximum level. O(mn log(mn)) time dominated by the sorts, O(mn) space with m*n <= 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: A floor of m by n cells carries a virtual height for every cell. Real heights must reproduce, within each row and within each column separately, both the equalities and the strict inequalities of the virtual heights, while cells in different rows and columns are unconstrained. The task is the smallest number of distinct real height levels needed, with the cell count up to one million.

problems.solution: Scan the scoreboard from rank 1 downward keeping a hash set of universities already represented; a team is a winner exactly when its university is new, and the first twelve such teams get the four first, four second and four third prizes. Because only the best-placed team of each university may be awarded and ranks arrive in order, the greedy scan is forced: skipping a new university could only be replaced by a lower-ranked team of the same university, which is never allowed. At least twelve distinct universities are guaranteed, so twelve teams always exist. O(N) time and O(N) space for N<=200 lines.
problems.statement_summary: A contest scoreboard lists up to two hundred teams in finishing order, each line giving the team's university and its name. Only the highest-placed team of any university may win a prize, and exactly twelve prizes are handed out. The task is to print the twelve prize-winning teams, in scoreboard order, given that at least twelve distinct universities appear.

problems.solution: Write S1(x) = sum_u d(u,x) and S2(x) = sum_u d(u,x)^2 inside a tree. Joining a in A to b in B leaves the two internal costs unchanged and makes every cross pair cost (dA(u,a)+1+dB(v,b))^2, so expanding the square gives cross(a,b) = M*S2A(a) + 2M*S1A(a) + N*S2B(b) + 2N*S1B(b) + 2*S1A(a)*S1B(b) + N*M. Two rerooting DP passes give S1 and S2 for every vertex of each tree in linear time. For a fixed b the a-dependent part is the line value S1A(a)*t + M*S2A(a) evaluated at t = 2M + 2*S1B(b) > 0, so building the lower convex hull of the points (S1A(a), M*S2A(a)) and querying it once per b answers everything in O(N log N + M log M) instead of the 2.5*10^9 double loop. Space O(N+M).
problems.statement_summary: Two trees of N and M computers are given; the cost of a network is the sum, over all unordered pairs of its computers, of the squared number of edges between them. Exactly one new cable must join a computer of the first tree to a computer of the second. The task is to report the minimum possible cost of the combined network, with both sizes up to fifty thousand.

problems.solution: A rotation of p_1..p_K is the near-identity permutation rho with rho(p_i) = p_{i+1} and rho(p_K) = p_1, because the new teacher-to-class map satisfies new_pos(t) = old_pos(rho(t)). Hence after weeks w1 < w2 < ... the map is rho_{w1} o rho_{w2} o ..., and answering 'teacher d in week x' means starting from d and applying the rotations from the LATEST week at most x downwards. Sqrt-decompose the week axis into blocks of B weeks; each block stores the composition of its plans as a sparse map keyed only on the at most B*K moved teachers. A query applies its own block's plans one by one and then does a single O(1) lookup per earlier block, O(B + M/B); an insertion rebuilds one block in O(B*K). With B about sqrt(M/K) both are O(sqrt(M*K)), so O(Q sqrt(M*K)) time and O(M + Q*K) space. A segment tree fails here: rebuilding the root costs O(Q*K) per insertion.
problems.statement_summary: N teachers start in the classes of the same number and are shuffled by rotations: a plan names up to ten teachers and, from a given week on, moves each into the class the next one occupied. Plans arrive in arbitrary week order interleaved with questions asking which class a teacher holds in a given week, counting only plans issued so far. Up to one hundred thousand operations.

problems.solution: Alob's corn field must be a mirror image of Bice's rice field, so the best area is area(A intersect mirror(B)) where A and B are the parts of the polygon on the two sides of the canal; the two sides give the same answer because mirroring is an involution. Decompose the polygon (oriented counter-clockwise) into signed triangles (O, p_i, p_{i+1}) with sign s_i, so that sum_i s_i * [x in T_i] is exactly the indicator of the polygon even when it is non-convex. Clip each triangle to the half-plane to get A's pieces and clip each to the other half-plane and reflect it to get mirror(B)'s pieces - all convex with at most four vertices - and sum s_i * s_j * area of the convex-convex intersection over all pairs. O(N^2) clips, O(N) space, exact for N <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: A simple polygon of at most one hundred integer-coordinate vertices is split by a straight canal line; one brother owns everything on one side and the other brother everything on the other, and these regions may be disconnected. The two brothers plant fields that must be exact mirror images of each other across the canal. The task is the largest possible area of one brother's field.

problems.solution: Call a position a barrier when a[i] <= m. A subarray has minimum exactly m with a single copy of m iff it contains exactly one barrier and that barrier holds the value m. Since all entries are positive, the best such subarray around a given m-barrier is the maximal one: it runs from just after the previous barrier to just before the next. So scan the barrier list once and, for every barrier whose value is m, take the prefix-sum of the open span between its neighbours, keeping the maximum. O(n) time and O(n) space per dataset, n <= 10^5.
problems.statement_summary: Given an array of positive integers and a value m, the task is the largest sum of a contiguous subarray whose minimum element equals m and which contains exactly one copy of m. The array holds up to 10^5 entries, each at most 64, and always contains at least one entry equal to m; several datasets follow.

problems.solution: Straight simulation. Hold the tree with a lexicographically ordered child map per node, a cached subtree size, and a parent pointer; MKDIR and RM add or detach a node and walk to the root adjusting sizes, which is cheap because those two commands number at most 5000. UNDO is a LIFO stack of records -- undo MKDIR by detaching the created node, undo RM by re-attaching the saved subtree (kept alive, not freed), undo CD by restoring the saved current pointer -- and the stack discipline guarantees the state a record reverts to is reachable. LS needs only the first and last five keys of the ordered map; TREE needs the subtree size plus the first five pre-order lines (walk the leftmost chain) and the last five (walk the rightmost chain), so no traversal is ever materialised. O(1) to O(depth) per command.
problems.statement_summary: Simulate a directory manager over up to 10^5 commands: create, remove and enter child directories, report a directory's subtree size, list its children in lexicographic order, print its subtree in pre-order, and undo the most recent successful create, remove or change-directory command. Listings longer than ten lines show only their first and last five lines.

problems.solution: A move replaces X by a proper divisor, and the number of prime factors with multiplicity Omega can drop to any smaller value, so each number is a nim pile of size Omega(X) and the whole list is nim -- but the last mover loses, so it is misere nim. The mover (RR) therefore loses exactly when some pile is >= 2 (a composite is present) and the xor of the Omega values is 0, or when every pile is 1 (all primes, since A > 1) and their count is odd. Sieve the primes to 10^6, run a segmented sieve on [A,B] to get Omega for each of the <= 10^5 numbers, then count subsets: a DP over the xor of composite Omegas (values < 64) combined with 2^(P-1) even/odd prime choices, plus the all-prime odd-size subsets. O((B-A) log log B + sqrt(B)) per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternate moves on a list of distinct integers, each move replacing a chosen number by any strictly smaller divisor of it, and whoever makes the final move loses. The opponent of the first player picks the initial list freely from the integers between A and B. The task counts the winning initial lists modulo 10^9+7, with B-A at most 10^5 and B up to 10^12.

problems.solution: Sort all 3N scores descending. Discard the N smallest outright -- each can be parked as the weakest member of some team without touching that team's median -- and pair up the remaining top 2N in order, so the medians are the elements at sorted positions 2,4,...,2N (1-indexed) and S is their sum. Correctness by exchange: in any optimal solution the largest score is wasted as a maximum, so it should shield the largest possible median, namely the second largest, and induction repeats the argument on the rest. O(n log n) time (or O(100) counting sort, since P_i <= 100) and O(n) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given 3N students with individual scores, a coach must split them into N teams of three; a team's performance is the median of its three scores and the total is the sum over teams. The task is to report the largest achievable total. Both N and every score are at most 100, over up to twenty datasets.

problems.solution: Count the complement: strings of length n over 26 letters that avoid p. Build the KMP automaton of p and keep only its |p| non-accepting states; the number of avoiding strings is the row sum of T^n applied to the start state, where T[s][t] counts letters moving s to t without completing a match. |p| <= 50 and n <= 10^12, so raise the transfer matrix by binary exponentiation, about 40 squarings of a 50x50 matrix. The answer is 26^n - avoid, all arithmetic mod M. O(|p|^3 log n) time, O(|p|^2) space; M is an arbitrary modulus up to 10^12, so products need 128-bit arithmetic and no inverses may be used.
problems.statement_summary: Given a length n, a modulus M and a pattern string p of at most 50 lowercase letters, the task is to count the lowercase strings of length n that contain p somewhere as a substring, reported modulo M. The length reaches 10^12 and the modulus 10^12, so up to twenty such datasets must each be answered without enumeration.

problems.solution: Every channel that is actually used costs E_ij to activate plus L to push the program across it, so give each edge weight E_ij + L; the set of used channels must connect every station to some pre-installed station, and a cheapest such set is a spanning forest of the graph in which the S initial stations are contracted to a single vertex. Run Kruskal with union-find after pre-uniting the S sources, summing the accepted weights. The network is connected, so exactly N-S accepted edges (post-contraction, N-1 unions minus the S-1 free ones) always exist. O(M log M) time, O(N+M) space with M up to 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: Stations form a connected weighted network; activating the channel between two stations costs a given amount, and afterwards transmitting the L-byte program across it costs L more. The program starts installed on S given stations and must reach every station. The task is the minimum total energy, with up to 10^4 stations and 10^6 channels.

problems.solution: For every subset S of the N <= 20 candidates, cost(S) = sum_j max_{i in S} a_ij. Write each max as a telescoping sum over prefixes: sorting topic j's students descending as v_1 >= ... >= v_N, max_{i in S} = sum_k (v_k - v_{k+1}) * [S meets the top-k set], so cost(S) = TOT - sum over (j,k) of (v_k - v_{k+1}) * [S is contained in the complement of that top-k set]. Bucket each weight on that complement mask, take one superset-sum (SOS) DP over 2^N, and cost(S) = TOT - G[S] for every subset at once. Sweep subsets by popcount for the per-K minima, so all Q queries are answered together. O(N*M + 2^N * N) time and O(2^N) space per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: A coach must teach M topics to a group of K students chosen from N candidates; teaching one topic to a group costs the largest of its members' individual times for that topic, and the group's cost is the sum over all topics. For each query value of K the task is the minimum possible total, with N at most 20 and M up to 10,000.

problems.solution: Preemptive scheduling of n jobs on m identical machines with release times and deadlines, which is feasible iff a transportation-style flow saturates. Cut the timeline at the sorted distinct r_i and d_i values (at most 400 boundaries, so <= 399 intervals) and build source -> job i (cap p_i) -> interval k (cap len_k, present only when [t_k,t_k+1) lies inside [r_i,d_i]) -> sink (cap m*len_k); a schedule exists iff max flow equals sum p_i, because any schedule induces such a flow and any flow can be realised. Realise it with McNaughton's wrap-around inside each interval: lay the per-job amounts end to end along a strip of length m*len_k and cut it into m printer rows, which never splits a job across two rows at the same instant since each amount is <= len_k. Dinic on ~600 nodes and ~80000 edges per dataset.
problems.statement_summary: Up to 200 files, each with a page count, a release time and a deadline, must be printed on m identical printers; printing may be interrupted and resumed on any printer, but a file may occupy only one printer at a time and each printer prints one page at a time. The task is to decide feasibility and, when feasible, emit an explicit schedule.

problems.solution: Let cap[i] be the water volume held when the surface stands exactly at the brim of wall i. Water enters at the left, so at that moment tank t (t <= i) is at level max(H_t..H_i), and every drowned wall t < i additionally carries a unit-wide column of water from H_t up to the level on its right. Building cap[] left to right with a monotonic stack of pools -- push each new tank, pop and raise every block whose level is below the new wall's height, merging widths (the wall itself joins the pool as a width-1 block at its own height) -- gives all N values in O(N) amortised, and cap is strictly increasing. A query K then answers count{ i : cap[i] < K } by binary search, strictly, because a reservoir filled exactly to a brim has not yet spilled. O(N + Q log N) time, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: A reservoir cross-section is divided into tanks by N unit-thick walls at given positions and heights; water pours in at the top left and spills rightwards over the walls. For each of up to 10^5 query volumes the task is the index of the last wall the water flows over, or zero. Positions reach 10^9 and volumes 10^15.

problems.solution: At water level h a ball of radius r either floats, displacing exactly its own weight w * (4/3)pi r^3, or sits on the bottom submerged to depth min(h, 2r), displacing the spherical cap pi t^2 (3r - t)/3; the physical displacement is the smaller of the two, which makes displaced(h) continuous and non-decreasing. The level therefore solves W*L*h - sum_i displaced_i(h) = V, monotone in h, so binary search h over [0, D] (about 100 iterations for 10^-9) and clamp at D when even h = D leaves net volume below V. O(n log(1/eps)) time, O(n) space, n <= 1000.
problems.statement_summary: A rectangular pool of given width, length and depth receives a fixed volume of water together with n spheres, each with a radius and a specific weight; heavier balls rest on the bottom while lighter ones float, and both displace water by Archimedes' principle. The task is the resulting water level, capped at the pool depth, to within 10^-4 error.

problems.solution: The price is the number of digits 6 or 8 occurring in the multiples of 8 up to n, plus the digits of n itself when n is not a multiple of 8 (when it is, it was already counted once). Count the first part with a digit DP over the <= 19 digits of n whose state is (position, value mod 8, tight, started), returning both how many numbers each branch completes and how many lucky digits they contribute; a digit contributes its own count times the number of completions below it. O(19 * 8 * 10) per query, O(1) extra space -- fast enough for 100000 queries, and n <= 10^18 rules out any enumeration.
problems.statement_summary: A staircase of n steps has its number engraved on every step whose index is a multiple of eight and on the final step; each engraved digit 6 or 8 costs a precious stone, and the tour price is the number of such digits. For a given n, as large as 10^18, the task is that price, for up to 100,000 independent queries.

problems.solution: Every empty cell uses exactly two of its four sides, and a side is used iff the neighbour across it uses the opposite side, so a valid layout is exactly a subgraph of the empty-cell grid graph in which every vertex has degree 2. The cost is 0 unless the two sides are opposite (left+right costs h, up+down costs v), i.e. the cost of sending 1 or 2 units horizontally out of a cell is convex (0 then h), which is expressible as two parallel unit edges. Colour the grid like a checkerboard: source -> black cell (cap 2) -> Hport/Vport through the (1,0),(1,cost) pairs -> the matching port of each horizontal/vertical neighbour (cap 1) -> mirrored white gadget -> sink. Feasible iff the flow saturates 2 * #black, which needs #black = #white; the min-cost flow value is the answer. O(V*E*flow) min-cost flow on ~1200 nodes and ~3200 edges with flow <= 800.
problems.statement_summary: Every empty cell of a grid up to 20 by 20 must receive exactly one pipe: a straight horizontal one, a straight vertical one, or a freely rotatable curved one, and the pipe ends must join so that all water circulates in closed loops with no leaks. Straight pipes carry per-cell costs; the task is the cheapest valid layout, or a report that none exists.

problems.solution: Colours are only ever copied, so the set of live colours can shrink but never grow: a necessary condition is that every colour of t already occurs in s (and for n = 1, s = t). For a connected graph with n >= 2 that is also sufficient, and the witness is built in two phases. Phase A repairs the colour multiset: while some colour occurs fewer times than t needs, take a vertex whose colour is in surplus, BFS to the nearest vertex whose colour is in deficit, and walk the surplus one edge at a time toward it, each move being a single vertex copying a neighbour; only surplus vertices are overwritten, so no needed colour is ever lost, and each unit of deficit costs at most one shortest path. Phase B permutes: with the multiset correct, match holders to targets and realise that permutation by adjacent swaps on a spanning tree, peeling leaves in reverse DFS order so the working part stays connected - a swap is one legal step because the update is simultaneous and both endpoints read the other's old colour. O(n^3) work, O(n) steps per repair, comfortably inside 20000 steps.
problems.statement_summary: Each vertex of a connected undirected graph carries one of k colours, and in one step every vertex simultaneously either keeps its colour or takes the colour of a neighbour. Given a starting and a target colouring on at most a hundred vertices with at most a hundred colours, the task is to decide reachability and, when reachable, print a witness sequence of at most twenty thousand steps.

problems.solution: Reconstructing the (unavailable) figure from the samples: the corridor is 0 <= y <= w, a shaft of width l rises above the ceiling gap from (0,w) to (l,w), door A is hinged at (0,w) and points (cos A, -sin A) into the corridor, and door B is hinged on a corridor wall further right so its tip stands l*sin B above that wall. A disc gets through a planar passage exactly when every bottleneck pair of obstacles is at least 2r apart, and here there are only two bottlenecks: entering the corridor past door A, which is the distance from the far shaft corner (l,w) to the door segment - l*sin A while the foot of the perpendicular lies on the door (A <= pi/2), else l, the plain shaft width - and squeezing past door B, a gap of w - l*sin B. So the answer is min(R, l*sin(min(A,pi/2))/2, (w - l*sin B)/2), O(1) per scenario, O(1) space.
problems.statement_summary: A circle of radius R starts far above a corridor of width w and must reach a point far to the right inside it, avoiding the walls and two hinged doors of length l, with the door length never exceeding the corridor width. For each of up to ten thousand scenarios giving the two door angles in radians, the task reports the largest shrunken radius that still gets through.

problems.solution: Clip each moving rectangle to the scene [0,W]x[0,H] (objects that drift off the picture stop counting - that is why waiting is said to help) and let f(t) be the area of the union. Sweeping in x, f(t) = sum over vertical strips of (strip width) times (measure of the union of the active y-intervals). While no two of the 2N+2 relevant x-coordinates - the object edges plus the clip lines 0 and W - swap, and likewise for y, each strip's active set and the merge pattern of its y-intervals are frozen, so both factors are linear in t and f is a single quadratic on that interval. Every order change is the root of a linear equation, so there are O(N^2) event times; sort them, and on each interval fit the quadratic from three samples and test its vertex along with the endpoints. With N <= 50 that is about 10^4 intervals times an O(N^2) union-area evaluation, and the minimum is exact rather than sampled. O(N^4) time overall, O(N^2) space.
problems.statement_summary: Up to fifty axis-aligned rectangles move at constant velocities across a photographed scene of given width and height. For any moment within the next E seconds a picture may be taken, and the task is the smallest possible area of the scene covered by the union of those rectangles at the chosen moment, reported to within a millionth relative error.

problems.solution: Building i is visible exactly when h_i exceeds every earlier height, so a prefix is summarised by (running maximum H, number visible so far) and the DP is over those states. With H fixed, an invisible building is cheapest at h_i = min(p_i, H), costing c_i*max(0, p_i - H) and leaving H alone (and it is illegal while H = 0, since heights are positive, which is why building 1 is always visible); a visible building may take any height above H and becomes the new maximum. The trap is that a visible building is NOT always best at max(p_i, H+1): lowering it below its preferred height can be worth it so a later cheap building can still clear it, so the candidate heights are p_j + d for |d| <= n - O(n^2) values - and the visible transition is evaluated with a prefix minimum over the running-maximum axis. That gives O(n^2 * n^2) = O(n^4) time at n = 70 and O(n^3) memory rolled to two layers; the answer is the cheapest state with at least k visible.
problems.statement_summary: Positive integer heights must be chosen for n buildings standing in a row, where building i costs its cost factor times the distance from its preferred height. A building is visible from the tram at position zero when it is strictly taller than every building before it, and the task is the cheapest assignment making at least k of the n buildings visible.

problems.solution: A subgraph of a tree that is a perfect k-ary tree is just a connected vertex subset, and since k >= 2 its root is the unique vertex of degree k (internal nodes have degree k+1, leaves degree 1), so counting each candidate at its root counts it exactly once. Let down[h][v][p] be the number of perfect k-ary subtrees of height h rooted at v that avoid the neighbour p; then down[h][v][p] is the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree k in {down[h-1][u][v] : u in N(v), u != p}, because the root must pick exactly k of its available neighbours and each must carry a height h-1 perfect subtree. The answer is N (the single vertices, h = 0) plus the sum over h >= 1 and over v of e_k taken over all of v's neighbours. Heights stop at log_k N (<= 17 for k = 2, N = 10^5), and evaluating e_k with one element removed for every directed edge is done with prefix/suffix symmetric polynomials rather than division, giving O(N k log_k N) time and O(N k) space modulo 10^9+7.
problems.statement_summary: A tree with up to a hundred thousand labelled nodes is given along with a value k between two and five. The task is to count, modulo one billion and seven, how many subgraphs of the tree are perfect k-ary trees, meaning they can be rooted so that every internal node has exactly k children and all leaves sit at equal depth.

problems.solution: Write each number as the exponent pair (a,b); gcd is the componentwise minimum and lcm the componentwise maximum, and the two exponents are combined by the same op, so values must be compared as 2^a*3^b. Any combining tree with k gcd-ops and N-1-k lcm-ops whose root is an lcm is exactly a partition of the N items into m = N-k blocks, taking the componentwise min of each block and the componentwise max across blocks (dually, the smallest outcome is m = k+1 blocks with max inside and min on top) - a brute force over all trees confirmed this family is complete. If m >= 3 two singleton blocks can carry the global maximum of a and of b independently, so the answer is the global componentwise max; m = 1 is the global componentwise min; only m = 2 needs work, and there the optimum is either a singleton block against the rest or the split induced by an a-threshold, both swept with prefix/suffix componentwise minima after one sort. O(N log N) time, O(N) space, and every scenario k is answered in O(1) from those precomputed arrays.
problems.statement_summary: Each of N numbers is given as two raised to some power times three raised to some power, and repeatedly two numbers are replaced by either their greatest common divisor or their least common multiple until a single number remains. For every count k of gcd merges from zero up to N-1, the task reports the largest and the smallest final value obtainable.

problems.solution: Within a round the worker's height never decreases, so the cells he touches at level h form one contiguous interval of the level-h occupied columns; hence a round is a root-to-node path in the tree whose nodes are the maximal intervals of {i : H_i >= h} for each h, i.e. the Cartesian tree of H by minimum (children of an interval are the pieces it splits into above its minimum). Every round entering a node's subtree places at most M of that subtree's cells and ends inside one child, so rounds(v) >= max(sum of rounds over children, ceil(cells(v)/M)), where cells(v) counts the subtree from v's base level upward; because cells shrink as the level rises, the whole chain of equal intervals collapses to its bottom level. That bound is achievable, so the answer is the sum of f(root) over the maximal runs of positive H, computed in O(N) time and O(N) space with a monotonic stack building the Cartesian tree.
problems.statement_summary: A worker must place a required number of horizontal bamboos in each of the columns of a vertical grid, building from the ground upward. In one round he carries at most M bamboos, starts at ground level, and may only move left, right or up, onto bamboos already there or ones he places, never descending while loaded. The task is the fewest rounds.

problems.solution: A cut whose heaviest crossing edge is at most W is precisely a union of connected components of the graph keeping only edges of weight > W, and those components are the components of the MAXIMUM spanning tree after deleting its edges of weight <= W. So the only candidate thresholds are the n-1 maximum-spanning-tree weights, and at threshold W the best denominator is best(W) = the largest subset sum of the component sizes not exceeding floor(n/2) (a union heavier than half is replaced by its complement); the answer is min over tree weights w of w / best(w). Unions of several components genuinely beat single components, so the subset sum is real work: build the max spanning tree with Kruskal and union-find in O(m log m), then sweep thresholds upward and evaluate the subset sum with a bitset over floor(n/2) bits, grouping equal component sizes.
