Pruning keeps it inside the strict limit: the running answer only falls, best(W) <= floor(n/2) means the sweep can stop once w/floor(n/2) reaches the current answer, a component larger than n/2 makes best = n - that size outright, and the greedy descending fit gives a valid lower bound (>= floor(n/2) - maxsize + 1) that tightens the answer cheaply before any exact DP is run.
problems.statement_summary: A connected weighted undirected graph with up to fourteen thousand vertices and thirty thousand edges is given. The slimness of a cut is the largest weight among the edges crossing it divided by the number of vertices on the smaller side, and the task is to report the minimum slimness over all cuts, within a hundred-millionth relative error under a strict time limit.

problems.solution: A closed tour exists for every board except a single line of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 or 9 squares and the 2x2 board; exhaustive search over the move graph confirms exactly that list (a lone row of 6 to 9 squares dies because two of its cells are forced onto the same pair of neighbours and close a short cycle). Every other board is built by tiling: cut the rows and the columns into parts of size 2 to 5 so that no 2x2 block ever appears (a part of size 2 is used only when that whole side has length 2), give each block its own closed tour, and splice the next block into the growing cycle by deleting an edge (u,v) of the cycle whose two ends lie in the neighbouring block, deleting an edge (u',v') of the block's own cycle, and adding (u,u') and (v,v'); the blocks are side by side so a legal pair of edges always exists. A single row with M >= 10 is done the same way from a base of 10 to 14 columns plus appended blocks of five, 1x5 being the only short line that works. The block tours are constant-size, so the construction is O(NM) time and O(NM) space, which is the size of the output.
problems.statement_summary: On a grid of N rows and M columns, each at most two hundred, the task is to visit every square exactly once in a cyclic order where consecutive squares, including the last and the first, are at Manhattan distance two or three, never one and never more. Any such tour may be reported, or a statement that none exists.

problems.solution: Build the Aho-Corasick automaton of the N taboo strings over the binary alphabet and mark a state bad if it ends a taboo string or if any state on its suffix-link chain does (propagated in BFS order). A binary string avoids every taboo string exactly when the walk it traces from the root never enters a bad state, so the clue length is the longest walk in the automaton restricted to good states. If any good state reachable from the root lies on a cycle of good states the clue is unbounded and the answer is -1; this is detected by the same DFS that computes best[u] = 1 + max over characters of best[goto(u,c)] over good successors. Rebuilding the string is a greedy walk from the root taking '0' whenever it still attains best[u], which gives the lexicographically smallest among the longest. O(sum of lengths) states, transitions, time and space.
problems.statement_summary: Given up to fifteen thousand binary taboo strings whose lengths total at most two hundred thousand, the task is to find the longest binary string that contains none of them as a substring, printing -1 when arbitrarily long such strings exist. Among all longest answers, the lexicographically smallest one must be reported.

problems.solution: The pairwise nested-or-disjoint condition makes the classes a laminar family, so inclusion gives a forest; the parent of a set is found in O(sum|S_i|) by processing sets in decreasing size and keeping, per skill, the deepest set seen so far (equal-size sets are disjoint, so ties are harmless). Covering the set S_v needs either one player of class v or one cover of every child of v, and the children route is available only when their sizes add up to |S_v| (otherwise the gap skills are uncoverable inside v). Hence g(v) = cnt[v] + min over children g(c) when the children tile S_v, else cnt[v]; a team needs one cover per root, so the answer is min over roots g(root), and 0 when the maximal sets fail to cover all n skills. The teaming is emitted by zipping the first g covers of each child, O(n + m + sum|S_i| + p) time and space.
problems.statement_summary: Given n skills and m character classes whose skill sets are pairwise nested or disjoint, plus p players of known classes, a team is a set of players whose classes together cover every skill and each player joins at most one team. The task asks for the maximum number of teams that can be formed simultaneously and one such teaming.

problems.solution: Problem p is forced first, so if its estimate exceeds 300 the team solves nothing and the answer is '0 0'. Otherwise the clock starts at t[p]; among the remaining problems, solving them in increasing order of estimate maximises how many fit in the 300 minutes (the classic shortest-job-first exchange argument), and for a fixed set the same increasing order also minimises the penalty because the penalty is the sum of prefix sums, which weights the i-th smallest by (k-i+1). The largest feasible set is also the set of smallest estimates, so one greedy pass answers both parts. O(N log N) time, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: A team faces N problems, at most thirteen, with distinct estimated solving times, and insists on attempting a designated problem first before working on the rest in any order. The contest lasts three hundred minutes and a problem counts only if it is finished by then. The task is to report the largest number of problems solved and, among orders achieving that, the smallest total ICPC penalty time.

problems.solution: Every minion is an interval [L,U] of acceptable temperatures and a room is one temperature, so this is the minimum piercing (stabbing) set of N intervals: pick the fewest points so that every interval contains one. Sort the intervals by right endpoint and sweep: whenever the next interval starts after the last point placed, place a new point at that interval's right endpoint. That point is the latest position that still stabs the current interval, so it dominates every other choice, giving optimality by the standard exchange argument. O(N log N) time, O(N) space, trivial for N <= 100.
problems.statement_summary: A company must house N minions, at most a hundred of them, in as few rooms as possible. Each room is set to a single temperature, and every minion accepts only temperatures inside a personal closed interval whose endpoints lie between one and twice N. The task is to report the minimum number of distinct temperatures needed so that every minion can be assigned to a room it likes.

problems.solution: Group each fruit's boxes into i maximal runs and knock out runs of length >= 2 by inclusion-exclusion; equivalently read off the Smirnov generating function 1/(1 - x/(1+x) - y/(1+y) - z/(1+z)). That gives ans = sum over i,j,k of (-1)^(A-i+C-j+M-k) C(A-1,i-1) C(C-1,j-1) C(M-1,k-1) (i+j+k)!/(i!j!k!), which is O(A*C*M) as written. Factor it: with a_i = (-1)^(A-i)C(A-1,i-1)/i! and likewise for the other two fruits, ans = sum_n n!*(a*c*m)[n], a single triple convolution of polynomials of degree <= 2*10^5. Two NTT products (three NTT primes plus CRT, or Kronecker substitution) give O(n log n) time and O(n) space with n = A+C+M <= 6*10^5.
problems.statement_summary: Boxes of three fruit types, namely A apples, C cherries and M mangos with each count between one and two hundred thousand, must be shipped in a single line so that no two neighbouring boxes hold the same fruit. Two shipments differ when some position carries a different fruit. The task is to count the valid orders modulo one billion and seven.

problems.solution: Binary search on R with the arc-cover decision test. If some disk of radius R covers K points, sliding its centre away from them until the farthest covered point sits at distance exactly R shows there is a witness centre on the circle C_i of radius R about some input point i. For a centre on C_i, another point j is covered exactly on an arc of half-width acos(d(i,j)/(2R)) around the direction i->j, so collect those arcs for all j within 2R, sweep their endpoints and compare 1 + max overlap with K. Feasibility is bounded by U = min_i d_{K-1}(i): R* lies in [U/2, U], and a square of side U/2 holds fewer than K points, so only O(K) points lie within 2R of any i. That makes a decision O(N K log K) and is exactly why the input promises K <= 20 or N <= 5000. O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: Up to a hundred thousand cats sit at distinct integer points of a plane, and one camera placed anywhere sees every cat within its visual range R. Find the smallest R letting the camera see at least K cats, where K is at most two hundred and, in every test, at most twenty unless the number of cats is at most five thousand.

problems.solution: Maintain the ingredients as disjoint sets. The invariant is that every group is either a single never-used ingredient or exactly the contents of one live cauldron, because brewing merges precisely the groups it consumes into the new cauldron. A recipe S is therefore brewable iff every group meeting S is contained in S, which is checked by collecting the distinct roots of S and testing that their sizes sum to |S|; if so, union them all and count the brew. Union-find with union by size gives O(sum(M) * alpha) time and O(max ingredient id) space, well inside sum(M) <= 500000.
problems.statement_summary: Recipes numbered one through N are considered in order, and a recipe is brewed exactly when its ingredient list can be assembled from ingredients never used before together with whole earlier cauldrons, each of which may be poured in only if all of its contents appear in that recipe. Brewing is compulsory whenever it is possible. With ingredient lists totalling half a million entries, count how many recipes get brewed.

problems.solution: A strictly convex lattice polygon is exactly a cyclic sequence of edge vectors with pairwise distinct directions summing to zero, so take primitive vectors (gcd 1, which forces distinct directions and hence no three collinear vertices), sort them by angle and take prefix sums. To make the sum vanish, use antipodal pairs {v,-v}; for odd N start from the three vectors (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1), which already sum to zero, and pair up the rest. Greedily take the pairs of smallest L1 norm, because the bounding box is exactly sum|a_i| by sum|b_i| over the chosen representatives. O(N log N) after an O(N) sieve of primitive vectors, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: Given N between three and four hundred thousand, the task is to output any convex polygon with exactly N vertices, every vertex at a lattice point with both coordinates between zero and forty million, all vertices distinct and no three of them collinear. Any valid polygon is accepted, in any vertex order, and the output is large enough that fast printing matters.

problems.solution: The configuration (cell, program counter) determines everything and the step map is deterministic, so the state graph is a functional graph on at most N*N*L <= 8*10^6 nodes. Walk it with first-visit timestamps until a state repeats, which exposes the rho's cycle, then replay exactly one lap and collect the cells actually entered. That block B repeats forever; if it is empty the robot has stopped moving and the trail is finite, so print 1. Otherwise the tail is B repeated, whose minimal period divides |B|, so take p = |B| - failure[|B|] from the KMP prefix function and answer p when p divides |B|, else |B|. O(N^2 * L) time and space.
problems.statement_summary: A robot starts on an empty cell of an N by N grid whose border is solid wall and repeats a program of at most N characters drawn from left, right, up and down, skipping any step that would enter a wall. Its trail records only the cells it enters. Print one if that trail is finite, otherwise the length of its eventual repeating block.

problems.solution: Only a hundred colours exist, so the multiset of colours in a subtree can be summarised by a 100-bit parity mask, and the number of magical colours is its popcount. Flatten the tree with a DFS euler tour so each subtree is a contiguous index range, and keep the per-position masks in a Fenwick tree whose operation is XOR; XOR is its own inverse, so the range mask is prefix(tout) XOR prefix(tin-1). A recolour is one point XOR of two bits. O((N+Q) log N) operations on two 64-bit words, O(N) space, for N <= 3*10^5 and Q <= 10^6.
problems.statement_summary: A rooted tree of up to three hundred thousand nodes has every node coloured with one of a hundred colours, and a colour is called magical for a subtree when it occurs an odd number of times inside it. Up to a million operations arrive in order, each either recolouring one node or asking how many colours are currently magical in the subtree of a given node.

problems.solution: The cost M + K/M over divisors M of K falls on (0, sqrt K] and rises after, and the two candidates M and K/M give the same cost, so the answer comes from the largest divisor of K that is at most isqrt(K). K has roughly 1200 bits and up to 10^10 divisors, so meet in the middle: split the prime powers into two groups with divisor counts as equal as possible (greedy over the factors e_i+1, each at most 101, so each side is about sqrt(D)), enumerate each group's divisors, sort the second, and for every d1 binary-search the largest d2 with d1*d2 <= isqrt(K). The cost is reduced mod 1e9+7 with a modular inverse for K/M, which is safe since every prime factor is below the modulus. O(sqrt(D) log sqrt(D)) big-integer comparisons, O(sqrt(D)) space.
problems.statement_summary: A customer needs exactly K bytes of storage bought as identical servers of M bytes each, where M must divide K, and the price is M dollars of base cost plus one dollar per server. K arrives as a string of two-digit prime factors, up to three hundred and fifty of them, and may have ten billion divisors. Report the least cost modulo one billion and seven.

problems.solution: Executives get consecutive blocks from the front, so the answer is the maximum number of parts in a left-to-right split of the array whose block sums are non-decreasing. Run a prefix DP that stores, for every prefix, the Pareto-best pair (largest number of blocks, and the smallest last-block sum attaining it): dp[i] takes the best j < i with pre[i]-pre[j] >= last[j], breaking ties toward the largest j so the new last block is as small as possible. More blocks never hurt and a smaller last block never hurts, so one pair per prefix suffices; the fuzz confirms this against exhaustive splits. O(N^2) time with N <= 3000, O(N) space.
problems.statement_summary: N briefcases, each holding some bananas, are handed out in order to executives ranked by evilness: each executive receives a positive number of the lowest-numbered briefcases still available. A more evil executive must end up with at least as many bananas as every less evil one. With N up to three thousand, the task is to maximise how many executives can be rewarded.
